screens.title: Incident Management and Post-Mortem Analysis
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we move beyond reactive troubleshooting and learn a structured approach to incidents that helps restore service quickly and prevent recurrence. You will learn the six phases of incident response — preparation, identification, containment, eradication, recovery, and post-incident analysis — and why each phase matters for enterprise networks where impact can be large. I'll also show practical techniques for root cause analysis like the five whys and fishbone diagram, and how to run blameless post-mortems that produce SMART action items. We'll ground these ideas with a hands-on scenario: a routing loop caused by an incorrect redistribution, and walk through how to document the timeline, probe deeper than an initial human error, and produce preventive tasks. Finally, we'll connect this to continuous improvement: better monitoring, configuration management, redundancy, documentation, and training. By the end you should be able to manage incidents with clear communication and to turn outages into repeatable learning that reduces future risk. Consider how your team currently shares incident duties and what would change if each outage produced a prioritized list of improvements.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: This chapter has targeted competencies that move you beyond fixing a single fault to improving the whole network lifecycle. First, you will understand each phase of a structured incident response process and why preparation and post-incident work are as important as triage. Second, you'll learn effective communication strategies during incidents so different audiences receive clear, relevant updates. Third, you will apply root cause analysis techniques — including five whys and fishbone diagrams — to identify systemic faults rather than surface symptoms. Fourth, you'll conduct thorough post-mortem analyses that produce SMART action items and continuous improvement steps. Each objective includes practical skills: writing a concise incident timeline, drafting a blameless post-mortem report, and translating findings into configuration changes, monitoring rules, or training tasks. Together these objectives help you reduce mean time to repair, lower recurrence, and build resilient operations. Think about a recent outage on your team and which of these objectives would have shortened the impact; that reflection will shape how you prioritize improvements.

screens.title: Why incident management differs from troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: Troubleshooting typically reacts to an immediate failure and focuses on restoring service as quickly as possible. Incident management is broader: it structures that reaction into phases and ensures the organization learns from the event. A key distinction is scope. Troubleshooting asks, what is broken now? Incident management asks, how did it break, who must act, how do we limit impact, and what prevents recurrence? For example, a congested link fixed by adjusting a queue is troubleshooting. Incident management will ask whether monitoring missed the trend, whether capacity planning is insufficient, and whether the change control process allowed a risky configuration. A common misconception is treating the post-incident report as optional or punitive; effective incident management treats it as the primary tool for systemic improvement. Practically, this means maintaining runbooks, assigning roles, recording precise timelines, and tracking action items to closure. When you combine fast restoration with disciplined analysis, outages become repeatable learning opportunities. Consider a recent fix you applied: could that one fix have been accompanied by an automated alert, a template change, or a training session to prevent the same issue next time?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Incident management organizes response and learning, whereas troubleshooting focuses on the immediate fix.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 10.10 › Why Incident Management
Definition & Contrast

Incident management is a set of coordinated phases that include preparation, identification, containment, eradication, recovery, and post-incident analysis. Troubleshooting is an essential skill inside identification and eradication, but on its own it doesn't guarantee prevention.

  • Scope: Troubleshooting fixes symptoms; incident management fixes systems.
  • Timeframe: Troubleshooting is immediate; incident management includes pre- and post-event work.
  • Outcome: Troubleshooting restores service; incident management prevents recurrence.
Concrete Example
Adjusting a queue to relieve congestion is troubleshooting. Documenting missing monitoring and adding an alert plus a capacity plan is incident management.
Key Takeaway

Treat each outage as both a service event and a source of systemic insight. Fast fixes plus follow-up actions reduce future outages.

Supporting Cards
Common Mistake
Skipping post-incident work because the service is restored. This delays prevention steps.
Pro Tip
Document the timeline during the incident; contemporaneous notes greatly improve RCA accuracy.
Check Your Understanding
Name one systemic change you could propose after your last outage and how you'd verify it worked.

screens.title: The six-phase incident response process
screens.narratorSegment: A repeatable incident response process keeps teams aligned during high-pressure outages. The six phases give structure and priorities so you can act quickly without losing sight of long-term fixes. Preparation happens before anything breaks: assemble a response team, define roles, maintain runbooks and network diagrams, and configure monitoring and contact lists. Identification is the first confirmed detection: validate the incident, determine scope, and gather initial evidence. Containment aims to limit damage — isolate affected systems, block malicious flows, or take a service offline temporarily while weighing business impact. Eradication is where you remove the cause: fix misconfigurations, apply patches, or revert a bad change. Recovery restores services and verifies stability with testing and monitoring. Finally, post-incident activity is the analysis and reporting phase: construct a timeline, perform RCA, and create SMART action items. A common error is skipping containment deliberation and making broad fixes that create more outages. The safe habit is to prefer reversible containment steps and to document every action so the post-incident timeline is precise. Ask yourself: which phase in your workflow needs stronger tooling or clearer roles?

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 10.10 › Six-Phase Process
Process Steps
Preparation
Playbooks, monitoring, roles, contact lists, diagrams.
Identification
Confirm incident, scope, and initial evidence collection.
Containment
Limit spread while minimizing business impact.
Eradication
Eliminate root cause, deploy fixes, patch or revert.
Recovery
Validate services, monitor closely, and finalize restoration.
Post-Incident
Timeline, RCA, lessons learned, and SMART actions.
Key Takeaway

Use reversible containment steps and contemporaneous notes to make RCA reliable and safe.

Supporting Details
  • Preparation reduces mean time to acknowledge by having ready contacts and playbooks.
  • Containment should balance risk: isolate only what is necessary and document impacts.
  • Post-incident activity turns temporary fixes into permanent system changes.
Common Mistake
Making irreversible changes during containment that complicate recovery.

screens.title: Preparation: playbooks, monitoring, and roles
screens.narratorSegment: Preparation happens outside crisis windows, and it's where you gain leverage. A good prep phase includes assembling an incident response team with clear responsibilities and backups, writing playbooks for common classes of incidents, and storing accurate network diagrams and configuration snapshots. Monitoring and alerting are part of preparation: tune thresholds so the tools detect true incidents rather than noise, and add alerts for leading indicators like route churn or C P U spikes. Another practical area is access and communication: maintain a current contact list for operations, application owners and management, and establish communication channels and templates so updates are concise. A common misconception is that preparation is a one-time activity — instead, treat it as living work: update diagrams after changes, rotate on-call duties, and rehearse tabletop drills. Example: before making complex routing changes, a prepared team will have a peer-review gate, a rollback plan, and an automation pre-check to reduce human error. A short rehearsal or checklist can cut incident time dramatically and prevent risky edits during emergencies. Preparation: playbooks, monitoring, and roles means preparation is ongoing: playbooks, accurate documentation, tuned monitoring, and clear roles reduce response time and risk.. In practical terms, what to prepare so incidents are handled quickly and safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 11 › Chapter 10.10 › Preparation
Preparation Checklist
Playbooks & Runbooks
Standard procedures for common incidents and step-by-step recovery instructions with verification steps.
Monitoring & Alerts
Tune alerts for meaningful signals and create leading-indicator rules: route churn, sudden CPU, or interface flaps.
Documentation
Maintain diagrams, contact lists, and configuration snapshots with change timestamps.
Example & Takeaway
Concrete Example
A pre-change checklist requiring peer review and an automated validation script would likely have prevented a routing redistribution mistake that caused a loop.
Key Takeaway

Small preparation steps — templates, peer review, pre-checks — significantly reduce the chance of high-impact incidents.

Pro Tip
Run tabletop drills and keep playbooks versioned with timestamps to validate your processes continually.

screens.title: Identification and containment strategies
screens.narratorSegment: Identification begins when monitoring or user reports indicate an event. The immediate goal is to confirm that a real incident exists and to scope its impact. Use quick checks: verify alerts, check reachability, and collect logs or monitoring snapshots. Avoid knee-jerk changes at this stage; instead, gather evidence that later supports a rigorous timeline. Containment follows identification and aims to limit the incident's scope. Effective containment balances rapid action with minimal collateral damage. Techniques include isolating affected segments, rate-limiting or blocking malicious flows, or disabling a problematic interface temporarily. Document containment steps, who authorized them, and their observed effects. A common misconception is that containment must be aggressive; too-broad isolation can escalate business impact. Prefer reversible actions and ensure rollback plans exist. Concrete example: if a routing loop is suspected, disable the redistributed route or interface that introduced it rather than globally shutting down routing on many devices. This limits collateral while permitting further investigation. The closing question: what reversible containment action would you take first in a routing-related outage? Identification and containment strategies means confirm with evidence, then contain with reversible, minimal-impact steps while documenting authorization.. In practical terms, confirming incidents and stopping spread without causing more harm. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Identification & Containment
keyIdea.text: Confirm with evidence, then contain with reversible, minimal-impact steps while documenting authorization.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 10.10 › Identify & Contain
Identification Checklist
  • Validate the alert and reproduce the symptom if possible.
  • Collect logs, monitoring graphs, and timestamps for initial timeline entries.
  • Estimate impact: services, users, regions, and business priorities.
Example Evidence
Routing table flaps and increasing CPU across multiple routers suggest a loop rather than a single link failure.
Containment Patterns
Isolate
Remove the faulty element from the topology, e.g., shut the problematic interface.
Block or Rate Limit
Use ACLs or policing to stop malicious or runaway traffic temporarily.
Fallback
Switch to a known-good configuration or route while investigating.
Common Mistake

Broadly disabling services without a rollback plan can increase outage impact. Prefer reversible, scoped containment.

screens.title: Eradication and recovery
screens.narratorSegment: Eradication is the phase where you remove the root cause identified during containment and identification. This might be correcting a misconfiguration, applying a patch, or restoring a known-good config. The important discipline is to verify the fix in a controlled way: test on a single device or a non-production segment, observe monitoring metrics, and ensure no collateral impact. Recovery is the formal process of returning affected services to normal operation and then validating stability over time. During recovery you should run verification checks, monitor for recurrence, and keep stakeholders informed. A common misconception is believing that a quick fix means eradication: a temporary workaround that masks the symptom is not eradication. For example, disabling an interface to stop a loop is containment; removing the incorrect redistribution and validating routing tables is eradication. After eradication, recovery includes bringing interfaces and services back, running health checks, and watching the system for an agreed observation window. Plan rollback actions and document the verification steps that prove the system is healthy. Eradication and recovery means eradication eliminates root causes; recovery restores and validates services with planned verification and monitoring.. In practical terms, removing causes and verifying full restoration safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 10.10 › Eradication & Recovery
Steps to Eradicate
  1. Confirm root cause with evidence and timeline.
  2. Implement the permanent fix in a controlled environment or single device.
  3. Run post-fix validation: routing tables, connectivity, performance metrics.
Concrete Example
Remove incorrect route redistribution, verify route tables converge, and run traffic tests before declaring recovery complete.
Recovery Checklist
  • Bring services back progressively using rollback controls.
  • Monitor for a defined observation period to ensure stability.
  • Notify stakeholders with resolution details and any remaining work.
Key Takeaway

Permanent fixes must be verified in a controlled way and observed over time to ensure eradication succeeded.

screens.title: Root Cause Analysis: 5 Whys and fishbone
screens.narratorSegment: Root Cause Analysis is about discovering why a failure occurred, not just what failed. Two practical techniques are the five whys and the fishbone diagram. The five whys iteratively ask why a condition occurred until you find a systemic cause. For example: why did a loop occur? Because an engineer redistributed a default route. Why did they do that? Because they lacked a peer-reviewed template and training. Continue until you reach a process or tooling gap. Fishbone diagrams categorize possible causes into areas like people, process, tools, environment, and equipment. This helps you avoid stopping at human error and instead find contributing factors across the stack. Timeline analysis complements both techniques by reconstructing events and correlating logs to identify the exact change that triggered failure. A misconception is stopping once the immediate human action is identified; RCA should push deeper to uncover missing policies, training, or automation. Concrete example: a routing loop traced to default route redistribution may lead to action items such as mandatory peer review, templated configs, and monitoring for rapid route churn. Close by asking: what categories would you include in a fishbone for your last incident?

keyIdea.title: RCA Techniques
keyIdea.text: Use iterative questioning and categorical analysis to find systemic causes and contributing factors.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 10.10 › Root Cause Analysis
5 Whys — Example Walkthrough

Start with the incident: "A routing loop caused a four-hour outage." Then ask why repeatedly until you reach a systemic cause:

  1. Why did the loop occur? — Incorrect route redistribution.
  2. Why was redistribution incorrect? — No filtering in the change.
  3. Why was filtering missing? — No peer review or template was used.
  4. Why was peer review absent? — Process didn't mandate it for this change type.
  5. Why was the process incomplete? — Change management lacked specific templates and training.
Fishbone Categories
People, Process, Tools, Environment, Equipment — use these to brainstorm contributing factors without stopping at blame.
Actionable Outcome
RCA should produce clear action items: mandate peer review, create templates, add monitoring for route churn, and schedule training.
Key Takeaway

Push analysis beyond the immediate human error to find process or tooling gaps that enabled it.

screens.title: Post-mortem analysis and the blameless review
screens.narratorSegment: A post-mortem is both a meeting and a document that captures everything useful about an incident. The report should be factual, chronological, and blameless. Start with a concise incident summary that states what happened, when, and the impact. Include a detailed timeline with timestamps for detection, containment actions, eradication steps, and recovery. Present the root cause and contributing factors derived from RCA. Then list lessons learned and SMART action items: specific tasks with owners, verification steps, and deadlines. The blameless approach is essential: it encourages transparent reporting and surface-level errors become signals for process or tooling gaps rather than reasons to punish individuals. A typical mistake is vague action items like "improve monitoring"; instead write "create route-churn alert with threshold X, owner Y, and verification by end of Q2." Post-mortems are also distribution documents: share a short stakeholders’ summary plus the technical appendix so each audience gets appropriate detail. Finally, track action-item closure. A post-mortem that sits in a folder and never leads to changes has zero operational benefit. Post-mortem analysis and the blameless review means blameless, factual reports with smart actions drive improvement; tracking closure turns insights into resilience.. Module 11 › Chapter 10.10 › Post-Mortem
Post-Mortem Template
Incident Summary
What happened, when, impact and duration in plain language for stakeholders.
Timeline of Events
Chronological sequence with timestamps, actions, and observed effects.
Root Cause & Contributing Factors
RCA output and fishbone findings presented clearly and without blame.
Action Items

Example SMART Item
Create route-churn alert with threshold 50 updates/min, owner: routing team, verify by generating controlled churn in lab and confirming alert within 2 weeks.

Post-mortems must produce tracked, measurable changes. Blameless framing produces honest analysis and better fixes.

screens.title: Proactive measures and continuous improvement
screens.narratorSegment: Post-mortem recommendations must be translated into proactive measures to reduce future outages. Key categories include monitoring and alerting improvements, configuration management, redundancy and resilience, documentation updates, targeted training, and regular audits. Monitoring: add early-warning rules for the same failure class and define clear escalation levels. Configuration management: adopt backups, templated changes, and automation with pre- and post-checks to catch mistakes before they reach production. Redundancy and resiliency: where single points of failure are identified, design for graceful degradation or failover. Documentation: update diagrams, runbooks, and contact lists immediately after changes so the next incident has accurate inputs. Training: run focused sessions on the protocols and patterns that caused the outage. Regular audits and tabletop exercises validate that the improvements actually work. A common mistake is issuing many vague recommendations and not tracking them; instead prioritize a small set of high-impact tasks, assign owners, and verify closure. Example actions from our routing loop: mandatory peer review, templated redistribution, route-churn alerting, and a training workshop on redistribution best practices. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we move beyond reactive troubleshooting and learn a structured approach to incidents that helps restore service quickly and prevent recurrence. You will learn the six phases of incident response — preparation, identification, containment, eradication, recovery, and post-incident analysis — and why each phase matters for enterprise networks where impact can be large. I'll also show practical techniques for root cause analysis like the five whys and fishbone diagram, and how to run blameless post-mortems that produce SMART action items. We'll ground these ideas with a hands-on scenario: a routing loop caused by an incorrect redistribution, and walk through how to document the timeline, probe deeper than an initial human error, and produce preventive tasks. Finally, we'll connect this to continuous improvement: better monitoring, configuration management, redundancy, documentation, and training. By the end you should be able to manage incidents with clear communication and to turn outages into repeatable learning that reduces future risk. Consider how your team currently shares incident duties and what would change if each outage produced a prioritized list of improvements.

This chapter has targeted competencies that move you beyond fixing a single fault to improving the whole network lifecycle. First, you will understand each phase of a structured incident response process and why preparation and post-incident work are as important as triage. Second, you'll learn effective communication strategies during incidents so different audiences receive clear, relevant updates. Third, you will apply root cause analysis techniques — including five whys and fishbone diagrams — to identify systemic faults rather than surface symptoms. Fourth, you'll conduct thorough post-mortem analyses that produce SMART action items and continuous improvement steps. Each objective includes practical skills: writing a concise incident timeline, drafting a blameless post-mortem report, and translating findings into configuration changes, monitoring rules, or training tasks. Together these objectives help you reduce mean time to repair, lower recurrence, and build resilient operations. Think about a recent outage on your team and which of these objectives would have shortened the impact; that reflection will shape how you prioritize improvements.

In this second objectives slide we'll focus on concrete skills you'll practice. You will be able to assemble an incident playbook: assign roles, prepare runbooks, and set monitoring thresholds. Next, you'll prepare stakeholder communications that avoid jargon and clearly state impact, ETA, and mitigation steps. You will also perform a systematic root cause analysis using techniques that scale to complex systems, and write a blameless post-mortem containing timeline, root cause, contributing factors, lessons learned, and precise action items. Finally, you'll implement continuous improvements like configuration backups, automation with pre- and post-checks, and monitoring rules that detect early signs of the same failure class. Each objective emphasizes measurable outcomes: checklists, peer review gates, and monitoring alerts that reduce recurrence. Practically, these skills mean your team can contain incidents faster, recover services safely, and each outage generates improvements that reduce future risk. As you learn, consider one policy you could pilot immediately to make changes less risky, such as mandatory peer review for routing changes.

Troubleshooting typically reacts to an immediate failure and focuses on restoring service as quickly as possible. Incident management is broader: it structures that reaction into phases and ensures the organization learns from the event. A key distinction is scope. Troubleshooting asks, what is broken now? Incident management asks, how did it break, who must act, how do we limit impact, and what prevents recurrence? For example, a congested link fixed by adjusting a queue is troubleshooting. Incident management will ask whether monitoring missed the trend, whether capacity planning is insufficient, and whether the change control process allowed a risky configuration. A common misconception is treating the post-incident report as optional or punitive; effective incident management treats it as the primary tool for systemic improvement. Practically, this means maintaining runbooks, assigning roles, recording precise timelines, and tracking action items to closure. When you combine fast restoration with disciplined analysis, outages become repeatable learning opportunities. Consider a recent fix you applied: could that one fix have been accompanied by an automated alert, a template change, or a training session to prevent the same issue next time?

A repeatable incident response process keeps teams aligned during high-pressure outages. The six phases give structure and priorities so you can act quickly without losing sight of long-term fixes. Preparation happens before anything breaks: assemble a response team, define roles, maintain runbooks and network diagrams, and configure monitoring and contact lists. Identification is the first confirmed detection: validate the incident, determine scope, and gather initial evidence. Containment aims to limit damage — isolate affected systems, block malicious flows, or take a service offline temporarily while weighing business impact. Eradication is where you remove the cause: fix misconfigurations, apply patches, or revert a bad change. Recovery restores services and verifies stability with testing and monitoring. Finally, post-incident activity is the analysis and reporting phase: construct a timeline, perform RCA, and create SMART action items. A common error is skipping containment deliberation and making broad fixes that create more outages. The safe habit is to prefer reversible containment steps and to document every action so the post-incident timeline is precise. Ask yourself: which phase in your workflow needs stronger tooling or clearer roles?

Preparation happens outside crisis windows, and it's where you gain leverage. A good prep phase includes assembling an incident response team with clear responsibilities and backups, writing playbooks for common classes of incidents, and storing accurate network diagrams and configuration snapshots. Monitoring and alerting are part of preparation: tune thresholds so the tools detect true incidents rather than noise, and add alerts for leading indicators like route churn or C P U spikes. Another practical area is access and communication: maintain a current contact list for operations, application owners and management, and establish communication channels and templates so updates are concise. A common misconception is that preparation is a one-time activity — instead, treat it as living work: update diagrams after changes, rotate on-call duties, and rehearse tabletop drills. Example: before making complex routing changes, a prepared team will have a peer-review gate, a rollback plan, and an automation pre-check to reduce human error. A short rehearsal or checklist can cut incident time dramatically and prevent risky edits during emergencies. In practical terms, what to prepare so incidents are handled quickly and safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Identification begins when monitoring or user reports indicate an event. The immediate goal is to confirm that a real incident exists and to scope its impact. Use quick checks: verify alerts, check reachability, and collect logs or monitoring snapshots. Avoid knee-jerk changes at this stage; instead, gather evidence that later supports a rigorous timeline. Containment follows identification and aims to limit the incident's scope. Effective containment balances rapid action with minimal collateral damage. Eradication is the phase where you remove the root cause identified during containment and identification. This might be correcting a misconfiguration, applying a patch, or restoring a known-good config. The important discipline is to verify the fix in a controlled way: test on a single device or a non-production segment, observe monitoring metrics, and ensure no collateral impact. Recovery is the formal process of returning affected services to normal operation and then validating stability over time. During recovery you should run verification checks, monitor for recurrence, and keep stakeholders informed. For example, disabling an interface to stop a loop is containment; removing the incorrect redistribution and validating routing tables is eradication. Plan rollback actions and document the verification steps that prove the system is healthy. Root Cause Analysis is about discovering why a failure occurred, not just what failed. Two practical techniques are the five whys and the fishbone diagram. Because they lacked a peer-reviewed template and training. Continue until you reach a process or tooling gap. Fishbone diagrams categorize possible causes into areas like people, process, tools, environment, and equipment. This helps you avoid stopping at human error and instead find contributing factors across the stack. Timeline analysis complements both techniques by reconstructing events and correlating logs to identify the exact change that triggered failure. A misconception is stopping once the immediate human action is identified; RCA should push deeper to uncover missing policies, training, or automation.
